title: Obfuscation Resistance Testing: How Well Can AI Identify Vulnerabilities in Intentionally Obfuscated Code?

original_idea.body:
# Obfuscation Resistance Testing: How Well Can AI Identify Vulnerabilities in Intentionally Obfuscated Code?

**Problem:** Real-world malware and exploit code is heavily obfuscated. DeepMind 2025 identified obfuscation as a systematic blind spot in AI capability evaluation. No benchmark specifically measures AI's vulnerability-finding ability as a function of obfuscation level.

**Direction:** Take 10 known-vulnerable code snippets (buffer overflows, use-after-free, SQL injection). Create 3 versions of each: (1) clean, (2) lightly obfuscated (variable renaming, dead code insertion), (3) heavily obfuscated (string encryption, control flow flattening). Run 3-4 models and plot vulnerability-detection accuracy as a function of obfuscation level. Identify whether there is a threshold obfuscation level that reliably defeats AI analysis.

**Why it matters:** If defenders can use obfuscation to reliably prevent AI from finding vulnerabilities in critical code, this is an actionable defensive recommendation. If AI is obfuscation-resistant, this changes the threat model for source code security.

**Relevant context:** DeepMind Rodriguez et al. (arxiv.org/html/2503.11917v3) identified obfuscation as a systematic evaluation blind spot. Assessing LLMs in malicious code deobfuscation (ScienceDirect 2024): LLMs can deobfuscate with ~70% accuracy. VirusTotal AI pipeline found 0-detection malware. CIPHER benchmark (arxiv 2602.01438) tested cryptographic vulnerability in generated code.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Direct measurement of capability gaps (obfuscation blindness, zero-day vs. known) enables realistic threat modeling for defenses.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires access to LLM APIs, security infrastructure, and sophisticated evaluation design. Likely beyond beginner capability.

title: Supply Chain Attack Simulation: Can AI Agents Identify and Exploit Poisoned Dependency Chains?

# Supply Chain Attack Simulation: Can AI Agents Identify and Exploit Poisoned Dependency Chains?

**Problem:** AI-generated code and AI coding assistants create new supply chain attack vectors (S1ngularity attack 2025 injected AI-powered malware into build systems). No evaluation measures AI offensive capability specifically for supply chain attack scenarios: identifying vulnerable dependencies, injecting malicious code into packages, or compromising CI/CD pipelines.

**Direction:** Set up a mock GitHub repository with a deliberately vulnerable dependency chain (using known-bad package versions from npm/PyPI audit databases, not real malicious packages). Ask AI agents to: (1) identify the vulnerable dependency, (2) craft a proof-of-concept exploit against a test application, (3) propose a realistic supply chain injection approach. Score each sub-task.

**Why it matters:** Supply chain attacks (SolarWinds, XZ Utils, npm poisoning) are among the highest-impact attack vectors. AI capability in this domain is completely unmeasured. The 2025 supply chain incident wave makes this urgently relevant.

title: Causal Analysis of Lateral Movement Failures: Why Do Models Stall After Initial Foothold?

original_idea.body:
# Causal Analysis of Lateral Movement Failures: Why Do Models Stall After Initial Foothold?

**Problem:** AISI and other evaluations consistently find models get initial access but fail to complete lateral movement and persistence phases. The causal mechanisms — whether this is planning horizon, tool invocation errors, or missing Active Directory knowledge — are not isolated.

**Direction:** Using a Metasploitable environment or HackTheBox easy machine, run AI agents and log every tool invocation and reasoning step. Manually annotate failures with root cause codes: (a) wrong tool selected, (b) correct tool, wrong parameters, (c) correct tool/params but misinterprets output, (d) correct execution but wrong inference about what to do next. Compute root cause distribution across 10-15 runs.

**Why it matters:** If failures are primarily (a) or (b) they can be fixed with better tool documentation or scaffolding. If failures are primarily (d), they require fundamental reasoning improvements. This failure taxonomy directly predicts which engineering interventions will most rapidly advance AI offensive capability.

**Relevant context:** AISI Folkerts et al. found NTLM relay and coordinated exploitation as bottlenecks. Context relay paper (NDSS 2026) addresses long-agent context management. AWS multi-agent architecture (2025) used specialized sub-agents to overcome single-agent lateral movement failures. Pentest-AI GitHub repository documents common failure modes.

# Multi-Language Vulnerability Discovery: Replicating Capability Findings Across Python, C, Java, and Rust

**Problem:** Most AI vulnerability discovery research focuses on C/C++ binaries or Python web applications. It is unknown whether capability findings generalize across programming languages with different memory safety properties and common vulnerability classes.

**Direction:** Create matched vulnerability sets: 5 buffer overflow variants in C, 5 equivalent logic vulnerabilities in Python, 5 in Java, 5 in Rust (focusing on unsafe blocks). Run models on all 20. Test whether capability is language-invariant or whether models have significantly higher performance on specific languages. Control for training data prevalence of each language.

**Why it matters:** If AI vulnerability finding is strong in C but weak in Rust, this provides a concrete signal that memory-safe languages offer durable AI-resistance even for offensive capability. If performance is language-invariant, language choice does not provide safety margin against AI auditing.

**Relevant context:** DARPA AIxCC processed 54M lines of code across multiple languages, finding 86% synthetic vulnerability coverage. LLM4Decompile focused on C. GitHub Copilot security studies (arxiv 2509.22040) focused on Python and JavaScript. CIPHER benchmark tested Python cryptographic code. title: Compounding Failure: AI Offensive Capability × Model Monoculture — When All Attackers Use the Same Model

# Compounding Failure: AI Offensive Capability × Model Monoculture — When All Attackers Use the Same Model

**Problem:** Two interacting failure modes: (1) AI offensive capability is rapidly advancing, and (2) model homogeneity means attackers and defenders are using similar or identical base models. If the attacker and defender both use Claude-class models, the attacker may have structural advantages from asymmetric objectives (find one path vs. patch all paths).

**Direction:** Set up a red-blue simulation where both the offensive agent and the defensive classifier are running the same base model (same API, different system prompts). Compare to a condition where they run different models. Measure whether model identity match between attacker and defender changes success rates, suggesting the attacker can predict defender detection logic.

**Why it matters:** Monoculture amplifies correlated failures. If attackers know the defender model family, they may be able to generate exploits that systematically evade its specific detection logic. This is a concrete interaction between the homogeneity problem and the offense/defense asymmetry.

**Relevant context:** SoK Potter et al. (arxiv.org/abs/2504.05408) documented offense > defense asymmetry. CrowdStrike 'AI vs AI arms race' (2025). Agentic AI Security paper (arxiv 2510.23883v1) on multi-agent risk amplification. title: Attack Trajectory Variance Analysis: Is AI Offensive Capability Deterministic or Stochastic?

original_idea.body:
# Attack Trajectory Variance Analysis: Is AI Offensive Capability Deterministic or Stochastic?

**Problem:** Models use stochastic sampling, meaning the same model on the same challenge may succeed in one run and fail in another. The variance structure of AI attack attempts has not been characterized: how many attempts does it take to achieve a given success probability, and does variance decrease with model capability?

**Direction:** Run 20 independent attempts of the same 10-challenge set using a single model at fixed temperature. Plot success rate distributions per challenge. Compute coefficient of variation. Test whether higher-capability models have lower variance (more reliable) or higher variance (more creative but inconsistent). Estimate the number of attempts needed for a 90% success probability.

**Why it matters:** If AI attacks are highly stochastic, attackers can achieve high success rates simply through repeated attempts — the 'best-of-N' threat model. AISI's single-attempt vs. 10-attempt scoring already hints at this. Characterizing variance structure is essential for realistic threat modeling.

**Relevant context:** AISI evaluated models with multiple attempt budgets. Claude Sonnet 4.5 went from 38% to 76.5% with 10 attempts (Mindgard 2026). AISI best run was 22/32 (single run out of multiple). Stochastic sampling in LLM outputs is fundamental but under-studied for security applications.

# Compounding Failure: Prompt Injection Vulnerability × AI Offensive Agent — Self-Sabotage During Red Team Operations

**Problem:** Two interacting failure modes: (1) AI offensive agents are vulnerable to prompt injection from adversarial content in their environment, and (2) red team AI agents browse target systems containing adversarial content. When a red team agent is hijacked by the target system, the attacker's own tool becomes the attack vector against the attacker.

**Direction:** Design a 'honeypot' CTF scenario where a target system contains prompt injection payloads in robot.txt, web page source, and service banners. Run an AI red team agent against the target and measure: (a) how often it is successfully hijacked, (b) what the injection causes it to do (ignore target, report false data back, expose attack infrastructure), (c) whether chain-of-thought scratchpad reveals injection detection.

**Why it matters:** This is a novel defensive countermeasure strategy: defenders can make their systems 'injection-booby-trapped' to neutralize AI red team agents. Demonstrating this works empirically would be a significant defensive contribution, and measuring the reliability of this countermeasure informs its deployability.

title: Zero-Day vs. Known CVE Performance: Measuring the Gap Between Knowledge and Novel Reasoning

original_idea.body:
# Zero-Day vs. Known CVE Performance: Measuring the Gap Between Knowledge and Novel Reasoning

**Problem:** Models are trained on data that includes CVE writeups, exploit databases, and CTF solutions. Their performance on known vulnerabilities may be dramatically higher than on novel or zero-day-class vulnerabilities. This gap has not been systematically measured.

**Direction:** Create two parallel challenge sets: (1) 10 challenges based on well-documented CVEs published before model training cutoffs (high likelihood of training data contamination), (2) 10 novel challenges implementing the same vulnerability classes but with distinct code and no published writeups. Compare solve rates. Test whether performance delta correlates with vulnerability class complexity.

**Why it matters:** If models significantly underperform on novel vulnerabilities vs. known CVEs, AI offensive capability is more limited than benchmark scores suggest. If the gap is small, models are genuinely generalizing — a more alarming finding. Directly addresses the contamination vs. capability question.

**Relevant context:** DARPA AIxCC (2025): teams found 18 previously unknown real-world flaws alongside 43 synthetic ones — suggesting some zero-day capability exists. LLM-CVX framework (ACM 2025) specifically evaluated CVE exploitation. OCCULT found models can answer 90%+ on knowledge tests (TACTL benchmark) but this does not imply novel exploitation ability.

# Formal Methods Transfer: Applying Model Checking to Verify AI Attack Plan Correctness Before Execution

**Problem:** AI agents generate attack plans that are often syntactically correct but semantically invalid (e.g., planning to exploit a vulnerability that doesn't exist on the target). There is no methodology for formally verifying attack plan feasibility before costly execution attempts.

**Direction:** Adapt lightweight model checking or specification language techniques (e.g., Alloy, TLA+ simplified) to specify a network state model. Before executing each step, use a programmatic constraint checker to verify the planned action is feasible given the current known state. Measure whether pre-execution verification reduces wasted tool invocations and increases net step completion rate.

**Why it matters:** Attack plan verification could dramatically improve AI offensive efficiency (fewer wasted attempts) — but also has a dual-use defensive application: using the same formal methods to verify that a planned attack cannot succeed before it is launched, enabling proactive defensive hardening.

**Relevant context:** Context relay paper (NDSS 2026) addresses long-running agent context management. AWS multi-agent architecture (2025) used specialized planning sub-agents. title: Experiment Variation: Temperature and Sampling Parameters as a Variable in Offensive Capability Benchmarks

original_idea.body:
# Experiment Variation: Temperature and Sampling Parameters as a Variable in Offensive Capability Benchmarks

**Problem:** AI cyber capability benchmarks are typically run at default model temperature settings. Higher temperatures may enable more creative (but less reliable) attacks; lower temperatures produce consistent (but potentially predictable) attacks. The effect of sampling parameters on offensive capability has not been studied.

**Direction:** Run a fixed 15-challenge CTF set on 2-3 models across 5 temperature settings (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0). For each setting, run 5 attempts per challenge. Compute expected success rate (mean across attempts) and peak success rate (best of 5). Plot success rate curves as a function of temperature. Identify the optimal temperature for maximizing offensive capability.

**Why it matters:** If there is a temperature regime that significantly boosts capability, this tells evaluators to test at multiple temperatures rather than just default settings. It also reveals whether deterministic vs. stochastic approaches to attacks have fundamentally different profiles.

**Relevant context:** Stochastic sampling documented as source of performance variance in AISI evaluations. Claude Sonnet 4.5 10-attempt success rate (76.5%) vs. single-attempt (38%) suggests retry strategies matter. CyberExplorer found models like Qwen 3 produced 'longer, more meandering attack trajectories' — possibly a temperature effect.

# Neuroscience-Inspired Capability Profiling: Dual-Process Theory Applied to AI Attack Reasoning

**Problem:** Cognitive science distinguishes System 1 (fast, intuitive) from System 2 (slow, deliberate) reasoning. AI models with extended chain-of-thought may be more analogous to System 2 (deliberate reasoning), while base completions are more System 1. Offensive tasks may differentially benefit from each mode.

**Direction:** Run offensive challenges under: (1) direct completion (no CoT, analogous to System 1), (2) short CoT (3-5 reasoning steps), (3) extended CoT (20+ reasoning steps). Categorize challenges by whether they require pattern recognition (System 1-favoring) or multi-step planning (System 2-favoring). Measure whether the benefit of extended CoT is concentrated in planning-heavy tasks.

**Why it matters:** If extended CoT disproportionately helps multi-step planning tasks (the hardest offensive bottleneck), this predicts that continued scaling of reasoning models will specifically accelerate the hardest attack steps. If CoT helps uniformly, the benefit is less targeted.

**Relevant context:** AISI found log-linear scaling with inference compute (reasoning tokens). Extended thinking models (DeepSeek-R1, Claude Thinking variants) show significant gains on multi-step reasoning. ARC challenge research on extended CoT. title: Cross-Model Consistency Analysis: Do Different Models Fail on the Same Challenge Instances or Different Ones?

# Cross-Model Consistency Analysis: Do Different Models Fail on the Same Challenge Instances or Different Ones?

**Problem:** If all frontier models fail on the same specific challenges, the failures may reflect structural limitations (fundamental task difficulty). If different models fail on different challenges, failures are model-specific (improvable with model-specific training). This distinction is critical for predicting capability ceiling trajectories.

**Direction:** Run 4-5 frontier models on the same 30-challenge CTF set. For each challenge, record which models succeed and which fail. Compute a 'co-failure correlation matrix'. Test whether co-failure patterns cluster by model family, task type, or both. Identify challenges where all models fail (likely hard tasks) vs. challenges with heterogeneous outcomes (model-specific weaknesses).

**Why it matters:** Universal co-failures suggest structural task difficulty that won't resolve with next-generation models. Model-specific failures suggest targeted training could quickly close capability gaps. This analysis is foundational for predicting the trajectory of capability improvement.

**Relevant context:** AISI compared 7 models across 18 months (arxiv.org/abs/2603.11214). CyberExplorer found distinct capability profiles for Claude vs. Qwen vs. Gemini models. CAIBench evaluated multiple models and found different degradation patterns. No published co-failure correlation analysis exists for cyber benchmarks.

title: Follow-up: Why Did Performance Accelerate in H2 2025? Attribution Analysis of the Cybench Inflection

original_idea.body:
# Follow-up: Why Did Performance Accelerate in H2 2025? Attribution Analysis of the Cybench Inflection

**Problem:** Cybench performance went from ~10% to 82% in 18 months with an apparent inflection point in H2 2025. The causes of this inflection are not understood. Was it model capability improvements, better scaffolding, increased token budgets, or benchmark contamination from training on CTF writeups?

**Direction:** Use publicly available model release dates, Cybench leaderboard data, and major scaffolding improvement announcements to build a timeline. Test three hypotheses: (H1) capability jump correlates with model releases, (H2) capability jump correlates with token budget increases, (H3) capability jump correlates with CTF writeup publication dates. Perform a simple regression analysis of performance on time-series variables.

**Why it matters:** If the inflection was primarily driven by contamination (H3), the 82% figure is misleading. If driven by capability (H1) or inference compute (H2), it is a genuine threat signal. # Compounding Failure: Rapid Capability Growth × No Standardized Evaluation Protocol — Incomparable Safety Assessments

**Problem:** Two interacting failure modes: (1) AI offensive capability is growing rapidly, and (2) no standardized evaluation protocol exists, so each lab uses different methodologies. Labs comparing their models against each other or against historical baselines are comparing incomparable measurements — potentially creating dangerous false reassurance or false alarm.

**Direction:** Collect methodology descriptions from 5 published AI cyber evaluations (AISI, DeepMind, OCCULT, Cybench, AIxCC). For each, extract: token budget, scaffolding type, target environment, evaluation time limits, success criteria, human baseline inclusion. Compute a methodology compatibility matrix. Propose a minimum standardization protocol that would enable cross-study comparison and test whether applying it to 2 studies yields more comparable results.

**Why it matters:** Without comparability, the field cannot assess whether safety evaluations across labs are producing consistent or divergent conclusions. This methodological inconsistency is itself a safety risk if it allows capabilities to be systematically underestimated through incompatible comparisons.

**Relevant context:** AISI noted no standardized longitudinal comparison methodology. Benchmarking Practices paper (arxiv 2504.10112) analyzed methodological variations. # Follow-up: What Happened at Step 22? Characterizing the Specific Failure Mode of the Best AISI Run

**Problem:** AISI's best run completed 22/32 steps — but the specific failure mode at step 23 and beyond is not publicly detailed. Understanding exactly what the model did at step 22, why step 23 failed, and whether this represents a recoverable state vs. an irreversible failure is critical for capability forecasting.

**Direction:** Using the published AISI paper's step description, reverse-engineer what step 22 likely involved (based on the ATT&CK phase sequence documented). **Why it matters:** The difference between 'model cannot do step 23' and 'model loses context state by step 23' has dramatically different implications. The former requires capability improvement; the latter is fixable with better scaffolding and already demonstrated in isolation. This distinction determines the timeline to full chain completion.

# Causal Chain Intervention: Improving Tool Documentation Quality as a Leverage Point for AI Attack Capability

**Why it matters:** If documentation quality is a major bottleneck, then the gap between current AI capability and full chain completion may be much smaller than it appears — improvable with simple engineering, not fundamental capability advances. This is critical for accurate threat forecasting.

title: Failure Mode: Context Window Exhaustion as a Safety Margin — Measuring the Performance Cliff

# Failure Mode: Context Window Exhaustion as a Safety Margin — Measuring the Performance Cliff

**Problem:** Long attack chains require models to maintain extensive context about the target environment. Context window exhaustion may be a natural safety margin for complex attacks. The performance cliff where context exhaustion causes catastrophic failure has not been measured.

**Direction:** Design a challenge set that progressively increases the required context: 5 challenges requiring 2K context tokens, 5 requiring 8K, 5 requiring 32K, 5 requiring 128K. For each challenge, have the model maintain a running state description of the simulated environment. Plot performance vs. required context size. Identify the cliff point per model.

**Why it matters:** If context window limits are a meaningful safety margin, then attacks requiring large state tracking are protected by current architectural constraints. As context windows expand (some models now handle 1M+ tokens), this margin will disappear. Knowing the current cliff point enables forecasting when it will be overcome.

**Relevant context:** AISI noted context management as a likely factor in long chain failures. Claude 3 context windows expanded to 200K. Context relay paper (NDSS 2026). CAIBench found 20-40% success on multi-step adversarial scenarios vs. 70% on knowledge. Context exhaustion is implicated in the AISI best-run ceiling.

# Follow-up to the Knowledge-Capability Gap: Which Security Domains Show the Largest Gap?

**Problem:** Research found that pre-trained knowledge of cybersecurity in LLMs does not imply attack and defense abilities — revealing a knowledge-capability gap. The magnitude and distribution of this gap across security domains (cryptography, web exploitation, network attacks, binary exploitation) has not been characterized.

**Direction:** For each of 5 security domains, create 2 matched question sets: (A) knowledge questions about the domain (multiple choice, analogous to OCCULT's TACTL), (B) practical capability tasks in the same domain. Run 3-4 models on both sets per domain. Compute a knowledge-to-capability transfer ratio per domain. Identify which domains have the largest gaps.

**Why it matters:** Domains with large knowledge-capability gaps represent safe harbors: even if models know about these attack types, they cannot execute them. Domains with small gaps are where AI knowledge directly translates to danger. This analysis directly informs where knowledge restrictions (training data curation) would be effective vs. futile as a safety measure.

title: Causal Chain: Does Scaffolding Quality Mediate the Relationship Between Model Capability and Task Performance?

# Causal Chain: Does Scaffolding Quality Mediate the Relationship Between Model Capability and Task Performance?

**Problem:** Evaluations use different scaffolding quality (tool wrappers, ReAct frameworks, context management). It is unknown whether observed capability differences between models reflect genuine capability differences or scaffolding quality differences that mediate performance.

**Direction:** Use the same base model with two scaffolding conditions: (A) minimal scaffolding (direct API call with simple system prompt), (B) production-quality scaffolding (ReAct framework, tool descriptions, state management, error handling). Run both on 15 CTF challenges. Measure the performance delta. Compare this delta to the inter-model differences reported in AISI and other evaluations.

**Why it matters:** If scaffolding quality explains a large fraction of inter-model performance differences, then capability comparisons across labs (who use different scaffolding) are confounded. This is a fundamental validity threat to capability evaluations and is directly actionable through standardization.

# Measuring the 'Overnight Attack' Threshold: Time-to-Compromise Distribution Analysis

**Problem:** AISI estimated 22/32 steps corresponds to ~6 of 14 expert-hours. There is no published distribution of time-to-compromise for AI agents across different challenge types, making it impossible to identify which challenges can be completed within operationally relevant time windows.

**Direction:** Run AI agents on 20 challenges spanning easy, medium, and hard difficulty. Record total wall-clock time, token usage, and tool invocation count per challenge. Plot time-to-completion distributions. Identify which challenge types complete in under 1 hour (operationally stealthy), 1-8 hours (overnight attack window), and >8 hours (requiring sustained operation).

**Why it matters:** An attack completing in under 1 hour may not trigger time-based anomaly detection. Attacks requiring sustained operation create higher detection probability. Understanding time distributions enables defenders to calibrate detection windows and tells evaluators which attacks are currently 'practically feasible' vs. theoretically possible.

**Relevant context:** AISI: best run estimated at ~6/14 expert hours. DARPA AIxCC: average remediation 45 minutes. NCSC: £65 per attack attempt. Cost-per-attempt data suggests mass deployment feasibility. No published time-distribution analysis across challenge types exists.
